steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting JCLEC-MO, a Java framework for multi- and many-objective optimization aimed at engineering problems. Motivate why engineers need such software, position it against existing metaheuristic optimization frameworks, summarize what JCLEC-MO offers, and close with the paper's organization.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Optimization in engineering and multi-objective metaheuristics
2. Many-objective problems and many-objective algorithms
3. Software suites and metaheuristic optimization frameworks (MOFs)
4. Existing MOFs: specialized vs. general-purpose
5. JCLEC as a baseline
6. JCLEC-MO: what this paper presents
7. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Engineering optimization
- optimization problems frequent in engineering; mathematical methods not always feasible
- growing use of efficient search methods, esp. problems with multiple objectives optimized simultaneously
- energy consumption, cost, time: paramount concern, conflicting objectives, deep impact on final solution
- metaheuristics like evolutionary algorithms (EAs), first single-objective, now multi-objective problems (MOPs): efficient transport systems, safe civil structures

2. Many-objective
- large number of objectives intrinsic to engineering problems; current techniques might not be efficient enough
- other communities too -> many-objective optimization approach
- variant of multi-objective optimization (MOO) for 4 or more objectives = many-objective problems (MaOPs)
- adaptations to MOPs/MaOPs share similarities: new diversity preservation mechanisms, indicators
- many-objective algorithms successful in engineering; specialized software tools appearing

3. Software suites / MOFs
- availability of software suites among factors most influencing engineers' choice; less coding, some guidance
- MOFs go further: collection of algorithms/code templates + utilities to configure and analyze outputs
- modular, adaptable; allow domain knowledge and constraints in representation/evaluation of solutions

4. Existing MOFs
- for MOPs: keep principles of MOO, adapt components to multiple objectives
- also efficiency, utility, integrability for broad industrial adoption
- specialized: jMetal, MOEA Framework -> larger catalog of recent algorithms
- general-purpose: ECJ, HeuristicLab, JCLEC -> ease of use, more components to represent/modify solutions

5. JCLEC
- mix of both: reusability, maturity, shorter learning curve + specialization for industry requirements
- JCLEC competitive: many customizable components, combined to solve user-defined problems
- easy integration via standards like XML
- core elements at high abstraction level: flexibility on stable platform
- good baseline MOF to extend for MOPs and MaOPs in industrial environment

6. JCLEC-MO
- extensible framework, search elements/techniques for multi- and many-objective optimization
- preliminary architecture only for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs); refined, new algorithm types, other metaheuristics
- generic metaheuristic models adapted to MOO; keeps general-purpose characteristics
- conceptual algorithmic model -> independence and scalability, distinctive
- competitive: catalog of algorithms, performance assessment, reporting
- case study: many-objective engineering problem; user-defined components; analyzing solutions e.g. with R

7. Organization
- Sec 2 background; Sec 3 existing frameworks; Sec 4 design criteria and architecture; Sec 5 functionalities and modules; Sec 6 case study; Sec 7 discussion vs other MOFs; Sec 8 conclusions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Optimization problems come up often in engineering, but because of their characteristics it is not always feasible to apply mathematical methods. So the use of efficient search methods has grown a lot in the last years, especially for engineering problems where multiple objectives have to be optimized at the same time. In engineering it often happens that energy consumption, cost or time, among others, need to be optimized jointly. All these factors are a paramount concern for the expert and they are conflicting objectives, and each one has a deep impact on the final solution. Metaheuristics like evolutionary algorithms (EAs) were first applied to single-objective problems, but they have been applied successfully to multi-objective problems (MOPs) in engineering, such as designing efficient transport systems or safe civil structures.

Recently it has been pointed out that having a large number of objectives is an intrinsic characteristic of engineering problems, and the techniques used now might not be efficient enough for them. Other communities are also asking for new techniques for more and more complex problems, and this has led to the many-objective optimization approach. This is a variant of the more general multi-objective optimization (MOO) and it is meant to overcome the limits of existing algorithms when problems with 4 or more objectives have to be solved, which are called many-objective problems (MaOPs). Each metaheuristic follows different principles to do the search, but the way they are adapted to MOPs or MaOPs has some similarities, like new diversity preservation mechanisms or the use of indicators. The resulting many-objective algorithms have been successful in engineering too, and specialized software tools have started to appear.

Actually, the availability of software suites is one of the factors that most influences engineers when they choose a solution or algorithm, since these suites can reduce the coding effort a lot and even give some guidance to engineers. Metaheuristic optimization frameworks (MOFs) seem to go one step further here, because they can include environments that do not just give a collection of algorithms or code templates, but also other general utilities to configure them properly and analyze the outputs. MOFs are modular and adaptable in different ways, and they should let users introduce specific domain knowledge and constraints in how solutions are represented and evaluated.

[Existing MOFs]
- for MOPs: keep MOO principles, adapt components; efficiency, utility, integrability for industry
- specialized: jMetal, MOEA Framework -> bigger catalog of recent algorithms
- general-purpose: ECJ, HeuristicLab, JCLEC -> ease of use, more components for solutions

[JCLEC]
- mix: reusability, maturity, learning curve + specialization for industry
- competitive tool, many customizable components; XML integration; high abstraction core
- good baseline for MOPs and MaOPs in industry

[JCLEC-MO]
- extensible framework for multi- and many-objective optimization
- preliminary architecture only MOEAs -> refined, new algorithms, other metaheuristics
- generic models adapted to MOO; conceptual algorithmic model (independence, scalability)
- catalog, performance assessment, reporting; case study, user-defined components, R

[Organization]
- Sections 2-8: background, existing frameworks, design/architecture, functionalities, case study, discussion, conclusions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Optimization problems come up often in engineering, but because of their characteristics it is not always feasible to apply mathematical methods. So the use of efficient search methods has grown a lot in the last years, especially for engineering problems where multiple objectives have to be optimized at the same time. In engineering it often happens that energy consumption, cost or time, among others, need to be optimized jointly. All these factors are a paramount concern for the expert and they are conflicting objectives, and each one has a deep impact on the final solution. Metaheuristics like evolutionary algorithms (EAs) were first applied to single-objective problems, but they have been applied successfully to multi-objective problems (MOPs) in engineering, such as designing efficient transport systems or safe civil structures.

Recently it has been pointed out that having a large number of objectives is an intrinsic characteristic of engineering problems, and the techniques used now might not be efficient enough for them. Other communities are also asking for new techniques for more and more complex problems, and this has led to the many-objective optimization approach. This is a variant of the more general multi-objective optimization (MOO) and it is meant to overcome the limits of existing algorithms when problems with 4 or more objectives have to be solved, which are called many-objective problems (MaOPs). Each metaheuristic follows different principles to do the search, but the way they are adapted to MOPs or MaOPs has some similarities, like new diversity preservation mechanisms or the use of indicators. The resulting many-objective algorithms have been successful in engineering too, and specialized software tools have started to appear.

Actually, the availability of software suites is one of the factors that most influences engineers when they choose a solution or algorithm, since these suites can reduce the coding effort a lot and even give some guidance to engineers. Metaheuristic optimization frameworks (MOFs) seem to go one step further here, because they can include environments that do not just give a collection of algorithms or code templates, but also other general utilities to configure them properly and analyze the outputs. MOFs are modular and adaptable in different ways, and they should let users introduce specific domain knowledge and constraints in how solutions are represented and evaluated.

When it comes to solving MOPs, these suites should keep the principles of multi-objective optimization by adapting their components to deal with multiple objectives. MOFs also still need to think about things like efficiency, utility and integrability if they want broad industrial adoption. Among the alternatives available now, there are some specialized frameworks like jMetal and MOEA Framework, whose main strength is a bigger catalog of recent algorithms. There are also general-purpose MOFs like ECJ, HeuristicLab or JCLEC, whose key advantages are other aspects like ease of use and more components available to represent and modify the solutions.

A mix of both alternatives would make it possible to take advantage of the reusability, maturity and shorter learning curve that general-purpose components bring, while specialization could bring the suite closer to the current requirements of industry. JCLEC has been reported as a competitive tool because of its large number of customizable components, which can be combined to solve user-defined optimization problems. JCLEC can also be integrated easily with other systems because it regularly uses standards like XML. Its core elements are defined at a high level of abstraction, which gives the flexibility needed to build new functionalities on top of a stable platform. So JCLEC is an interesting baseline MOF to extend with different metaheuristics for solving both MOPs and MaOPs in an industrial environment.

For this, this paper presents JCLEC-MO, an extensible framework that provides suitable search elements and techniques for multi- and many-objective optimization. The preliminary architecture was only focused on multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs), and it has been refined and evolved a lot to include new types of algorithms and support for other metaheuristics. So JCLEC-MO provides generic metaheuristic models that are adapted to the precepts of MOO, and it still keeps the valuable characteristics of a general-purpose solution. A distinctive characteristic of JCLEC-MO is the conceptual algorithmic model, which was proposed to achieve independence and significant scalability. It is also competitive in the catalog of algorithms, the mechanisms to assess their performance and the reporting capabilities. A case study shows how this suite can solve a many-objective engineering problem, and it illustrates how user-defined components should be designed and how the returned solutions can be analyzed, e.g. with R functionalities.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 gives the essential background on metaheuristics for multi- and many-objective optimization and on MOFs. Section 3 analyzes existing frameworks for solving multi-objective problems. Section 4 presents the design criteria and the architecture of JCLEC-MO. Section 5 describes the software functionalities and its modular organization in more detail. Section 6 develops an illustrative case study to show how JCLEC-MO can be applied and used as a supportive tool for engineers. Section 7 discusses the benefits of JCLEC-MO compared to other available MOFs, and finally Section 8 outlines the conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Optimization problems frequently appear in the engineering field, but their characteristics make the application of mathematical methods not always feasible [1]. Hence, the use of efficient search methods has grown significantly in the last years, especially for those engineering problems where multiple objectives need to be optimized simultaneously [2]. A recurrent situation in engineering is the need to jointly optimize energy consumption, cost or time, among others. All these factors are a paramount concern to the expert and represent conflicting objectives, each one having a deep impact on the final solution [2]. Initially applied to single-objective problems, metaheuristics like evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have been successfully applied to multi-objective problems (MOPs) in engineering, such as the design of efficient transport systems [3] or safe civil structures [4].

The presence of a large number of objectives has recently been pointed out as an intrinsic characteristic of engineering problems [1], for which the currently applied techniques might not be efficient enough. Other communities are also demanding novel techniques to face increasingly complex problems, which has led to the appearance of the many-objective optimization approach [5,6]. This variant of the more general multi-objective optimization (MOO) is specifically devoted to overcoming the limits of existing algorithms when problems with 4 or more objectives, known as many-objective problems (MaOPs), have to be faced. Even though each metaheuristic follows different principles to conduct the search, their adaptations to deal with either MOPs or MaOPs share some similarities, such as new diversity preservation mechanisms or the use of indicators [6,7]. The resulting many-objective algorithms have proven successful in the engineering field too [8,9,10], where specialized software tools have begun to appear [11].

In fact, the availability of software suites is one of the factors that most influences engineers when selecting a solution or algorithm [2], as they can greatly reduce coding efforts and even provide some guidance to engineers. In this context, metaheuristic optimization frameworks (MOFs) [12] go one step further, as they may integrate environments that provide not only a collection of algorithms or code templates, but also other general utilities to properly configure them and analyze outputs. MOFs are modular and adaptable in different ways, and should enable the introduction of specific domain knowledge and constraints in the representation and evaluation of solutions [9,1].

Focusing on the resolution of MOPs, these suites are expected to keep the principles of multi-objective optimization by adapting their components to deal with multiple objectives. At the same time, MOFs still need to consider aspects like efficiency, utility and integrability if broad industrial adoption is sought. Among the currently available alternatives, there are specialized frameworks like jMetal [13] and MOEA Framework [14], whose main strength lies in a more extensive catalog of recent algorithms. Other general-purpose MOFs like ECJ [15], HeuristicLab [16] or JCLEC [17] stand out in other aspects, with ease of use and a greater availability of components to represent and modify solutions as their key advantages.

A mix of both alternatives would make it possible to take advantage of the reusability, maturity and reduced learning curve promoted by general-purpose components, whereas specialization might bring the suite closer to the current requirements of industry. In this regard, JCLEC has been reported as a competitive tool due to its large number of customizable components, which can be combined to solve user-defined optimization problems [12]. In addition, JCLEC can be easily integrated with other systems because of its regular use of standards like XML. Its core elements are defined at a high level of abstraction, providing the flexibility required to build new functionalities on top of a stable platform. Therefore, JCLEC is an interesting baseline MOF to be extended with different metaheuristics for the resolution of both MOPs and MaOPs within an industrial environment.

To this end, this paper presents JCLEC-MO, an extensible framework providing suitable search elements and techniques for multi- and many-objective optimization. The preliminary architecture [18], focused only on multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs), has been refined and significantly evolved to include new types of algorithms and support for other metaheuristics. As a result, JCLEC-MO provides generic metaheuristic models conveniently adapted to the precepts of MOO, while preserving the valuable characteristics of a general-purpose solution. The conceptual algorithmic model proposed to achieve independence and significant scalability is a distinctive characteristic of JCLEC-MO. It is also competitive in terms of its catalog of algorithms, the mechanisms to assess their performance and its reporting capabilities. A case study shows how this suite enables the resolution of a many-objective engineering problem, illustrating how user-defined components should be conceived and how the returned solutions can be analyzed, e.g. by using R functionalities.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides essential background on metaheuristics for multi- and many-objective optimization and on MOFs. Existing frameworks for solving multi-objective problems are analyzed in Section 3. Section 4 presents the design criteria and architecture of JCLEC-MO, and Section 5 provides a more detailed description of the software functionalities and its modular organization. Section 6 then develops an illustrative case study showing the applicability and use of JCLEC-MO as a supportive tool for engineers. A discussion of the benefits of JCLEC-MO compared to other available MOFs is presented in Section 7, and conclusions are outlined in Section 8.

References:
[1] Singh [2016] Singh, H.K., 2016. Development of optimization methods to deal with current challenges in engineering design optimization. AI Communications 29, 219–221. doi: 10.3233/AIC-140645 .
[2] Marler and Arora [2004] Marler, R., Arora, J., 2004. Survey of multi-objective optimization methods for engineering. Struct. Multidiscipl. Optim. 26, 369–395. doi: 10.1007/s00158-003-0368-6 .
